label: Geometric Selection Theorems
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 207 through 230, asks a deceptively simple question: given many points in the plane or in higher dimensions, must some single point be deeply covered by the simplices they span? The selection theorems answer yes, with quantitative force, and seed an entire theory.

label: From One Point to Many Simplices
notes: A finite set of n points in d dimensions spans roughly n to the power d plus one simplices. The first selection lemma promises one location pierced by a constant fraction of them. We set up the counting that makes such a universal heavily covered point believable.

label: The First Selection Lemma
notes: The first selection lemma is the chapter's cornerstone. For every dimension there is a positive constant so that some point lies inside at least that fraction of all simplices spanned by the set. The constant depends only on dimension, never on the number of points.

label: Proof Idea via Centerpoints
notes: The planar proof routes through the centerpoint theorem. A centerpoint sits behind a constant fraction of points across every direction, and a Radon or Tverberg style partition then certifies that many spanned triangles must wrap around it, giving the desired deep point.

label: Order Types and Same-Type
notes: To control configurations combinatorially we record only orientation signs, the order type. Two tuples have the same type when corresponding simplices share orientations. This discrete fingerprint lets us argue about geometry through finite, checkable data rather than exact coordinates.

label: The Same-Type Lemma
notes: The same-type lemma says any large point set hides large subsets, one per color class, so that every transversal picks the same order type. Positive fractions survive, so the structure is not rare. This regularity is the engine behind the second selection lemma.

label: The Second Selection Lemma
notes: The second selection lemma upgrades the first. Take only a dense family of simplices, an alpha fraction of all of them, and still some point is pierced by a positive fraction of that family. The covering bound degrades polynomially in alpha but never vanishes.

label: Hypergraph Regularity
notes: The proof packages simplices as a hypergraph and applies a geometric regularity decomposition. The same-type lemma supplies dense homogeneous blocks where every simplex behaves alike, so a single point inherited from one block pierces a guaranteed share of the dense family.

label: Positive-Fraction Selection
notes: Positive-fraction Tverberg sharpens the picture. Inside any large set there are linearly many disjoint blocks whose every transversal simplex contains one common point. We thus get not just one deep point but a robust, perturbation-stable bundle of containments to exploit.

label: Application to k-Sets
notes: Selection lemmas feed the k-set problem. Bounding how many ways a hyperplane can split n points into a fixed size part uses the second selection lemma to translate many halving structures into a heavily covered point, then counts the contradiction it forces.

label: Invariants and Sanity Checks
notes: The notebook turns these theorems into executable invariants: convex hulls, orientation determinants, and Vandermonde collisions that vanish on degeneracy. Watching a determinant change sign is exactly the order-type flip the same-type lemma forbids inside its homogeneous blocks.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We close by chaining the results: first selection gives one deep point, the same-type lemma gives regularity, second selection survives sparsification, and positive-fraction Tverberg gives robust bundles. Together they underpin k-set bounds and the incidence machinery of later chapters.
